Deposit your discs

Post a disc in and it joins the vault as one more copy other people can borrow. Depositing makes your membership free, and you can recall any disc you own at any time.

Nothing is posted anywhere. This prototype adds the copy straight to the shelf so you can see what happens.

What happens to your disc

  1. We catalogue it and give it a shelf tag.
  2. It sits in the vault, and only one person can borrow it at a time.
  3. Borrowers stream it. Nobody keeps a copy, and nothing is downloaded.
  4. Ask for it back and it leaves circulation on the spot.
1 disc = 1 loan

How it works

Shelf Life takes the thing libraries have always done and moves it online, without pretending the copy limit does not matter.

Step one

Deposit or subscribe

Send in discs and borrow free, or pay a small monthly fee and borrow from the whole vault.

Step two

One copy, one borrower

Every physical copy unlocks a single digital loan. When it is out, you join the queue, the same as a library hold.

Step three

Stream, then return

Loans run fourteen days and stream rather than download, so no extra copy exists when the loan ends.

Step four

Recall anytime

Your discs stay yours. Ask for one back and it leaves circulation and gets posted home.

Is this legal? Not yet.

Courts rejected a version of the one-copy argument in Zediva (2011), Aereo (2014), ReDigi (2018) and Hachette v. Internet Archive (2024), and Australian law prohibits breaking the copy protection on a disc. Shelf Life is a student project: speculative design that argues lending law should catch up, not a service you can sign up to.

Why these titles

Everything in the vault is out of print, delisted, tangled in licensing, or gone altogether. Three of the films are marked lost: no copy survives to lend, which is the part no lending service can fix. A 2023 study by the Video Game History Foundation found 87% of classic US games released before 2010 are out of print.
